explanation: Fires on boilerplate and structural tokens in technical text: the last seconds digit of timestamps in email or RSS date headers (e.g. '17:34:3[3] +000'), and code or header keywords such as class names after 'class', '@version', 'using System;', 'rights reserved', '<li>', and query-string terms. These seem loosely tied together as 'formulaic header/metadata' positions, but they don't share one clear story. Ordinary prose barely activates it.

Fires strongly on the subword 'pro'/'Pro'/'PRO' at the start of a word, in any language or casing (Protest, Problem, Prozentsatz, progesterone, prohibited, procyon). Weaker on similar onsets such as 'pr', 'prox', 'prop', 'RO' and 'Gro'. Whole words like 'protocol' or 'producer' tokenized as one piece fire only weakly.

Fires on function words and slots inside quantitative or measurement phrases, just before or around a number or extent: 'no more', 'at its narrowest', 'at least', 'in diameter', 'in the US', the space before a day number in 'December[ ]31', 'height[:]'. Strongest when the token links a quantity to its unit, scope or date. Generic prepositions with no quantity nearby fire weakly.

Mixed. It fires on word-initial subword pieces of scientific terms ('gluc' in glucocorticoid, 'micro[s]urgical', 'Vit'rectomy), on 'one' in 'nearly one million' or 'one of', on HTML '<form' tokens, and on assorted code and name tokens. No single feature predicts it reliably.

Fires on closing brackets and delimiters that end a parenthetical or nested group: ')' or '-)' closing an aside in prose ('(non-)degenerate', '(or decrease)'), '}}' in LaTeX, '>>' in generics, ']}', closing '**' or '_' markup, and closing quotes. Strongest for a close-paren ending a short in-word or in-phrase parenthetical; opening brackets don't fire.

Fires on tokens in the middle of non-English text, especially verbs, auxiliaries and particles in French, German, Portuguese, Russian, Finnish and Japanese (e.g. 'J'ai', 'muss', 'avons', 'под', Japanese particles). Weaker on code tokens such as indentation, ';' and '?' in JavaScript. English prose barely fires.

No clear pattern. It fires on things like 'Max' in minMaxIdx, '8' in ISO-8859, '9' in Itanium 9700, 'Z' at the start of names (Zune, Zelenskiy), 'IL' in gene names, 'Property' in PropertyGroup, 'include'/'division' after 'multiple access', and odd subword pieces. These look like a mix of name/identifier pieces and unrelated contexts.

Fires mostly on subword pieces in the middle of proper nouns and foreign place or person names (Vo[iv]odeship, Ta[orm]ina, T[ama]ulipas, Hart[mut], WY[OM]ING), and on tokens inside sports or encyclopedic fact phrases ('Under 18's', '3 m springboard', 'K-2', scores). Typical of Wikipedia-style biographical and geographic text. Common English words fire only weakly.

Fires on the noun naming the counted group right after a numeral or quantifier, above all 'people' in phrases like 'killed 17 people', 'employs 95 people' or 'home to 9,800 people'. Also fires on similar nouns (members, inhabitants, individuals, views, pupils) and on 'died' after 'N people'. Weak without a preceding number or quantity.

Fires on the second or later subword of a class or module name right after the 'class'/'module'/'interface' keyword in code, e.g. 'Request' in 'class DescribeDrdsComponentsRequest', 'Controller', 'Test', 'Manager'. Also fires on the bare name after 'class'. Weaker on section headings such as 'Introduction' or 'Teams'.

Mixed. It fires on subword pieces in names and legal citation text ('Circuit Judges', 'SOP[H]OMORE', 'G[ERN]ON'), on 'way' in 'no way' and 'all' in 'makes it all possible' or 'all together', on ')' closing abbreviation definitions, and on other pieces. No single shared feature.

Fires on number tokens in durations, ages and dates, mainly the second digit of a two-digit number ('2[7] month period', 'the 2[6] years old', '3[6]0 degree') and number words in 'over a three-year period' or 'a half year'. Also fires on some legal-citation tokens ('PER C', 'were on the brief'). Number contexts dominate.

Mixed. It fires on the space between CSS padding values ('padding: 0[ ]0'), on pharmacology subwords ('beta-block', 'antico[ag]ulant', 'monoclon[al]', 'absorption'), on 'Rewrite' in htaccess rules, and on assorted others. Several unrelated clusters.

Mixed. It fires on mid-word subword pieces in scientific and proper names (nucle[os]ide, [Ap]odemus, plasminogen activ-ator, TOR-ONTO), on 'was'/'can' in first-person prose, on 'A' in Q&A 'A:' and on code-syntax tokens. No coherent single trigger.

Fires on determiners and function words right after a preposition or verb that opens a noun phrase, mostly 'the', 'a', 'an' and 'of' in phrases like 'one of the', 'a set of', 'hosted an', 'for example'. Strongest early in a sentence or document. Determiners deep in long text fire weakly.

Fires in code at the start of an 'else' branch or at block-closing positions: 'else' after '}', 'default' in switch statements, '#else' in the C preprocessor, and the indentation whitespace before a closing '}' or the next branch. Prose words like 'before' or 'since' fire only weakly.

Fires on the connector after a time or place head word: 'of' in 'first Wednesday of', 'Isle of', 'head of', 'last cell of'; the comma after weekdays ('On Thursday,'); and the comma between town and state. Mostly the token that follows a date, weekday or place name in news or event text.

Fires on content words in biomedical abstracts, especially disease, clinical and method terms or their first subword (bioterrorism, schizophrenia, 'confirm', 'purulent', 'drug user', 'Kaplan-Meier', 'QT'). Mostly medical or biological terminology; generic words fire weakly.

Fires on coordinating 'and', 'or' and commas that join items in a list or two coordinated nouns or clauses ('39 (+/-2.6) and 29', 'E45 or Aqueous cream', 'the tables and fields,'). Strongest right after the first conjunct of a list or pair.

Fires on tokens inside technical compound terms in scientific and patent writing, mostly subword or modifier pieces in the middle of a term (py[rim]idine, annular[-shaped], spirally[-w]ound, de[hum]idifier, [micro]vessel, [medial] epicondyles), and on commas in scientific lists. A broad 'technical term continuation' feature.

Fires on punctuation and function words in formal or archaic registers: scripture and quoted speech ('?', ',', '!', 'of' in Bible or Qur'an quotes) and patent boilerplate ('of the present invention', 'Field of the Invention', 'of this type'). These two registers make two related jobs.
